narrative: Fire ecology work this week bridged planning and impact: a Conservation Biology piece calls for folding biodiversity protection into emergency management after megafires, while a Global Change Biology study documents escalating winter fire-weather risk in the southwestern US linked to anthropogenic warming, and a companion paper shows fire-driven disturbance mosaics reshaping pollinator communities across managed forests. Climate-themed papers converge on vulnerability of specialised systems, from Europe's mountain flora facing range collapse to karst vegetation showing amplified phenological sensitivity relative to non-karst landscapes. Movement and connectivity research remains a strong thread, with new corridor-prioritisation work for jaguars across the Americas and for tigers, leopards and elephants in southern India, alongside fine-scale habitat segregation in a southern-range polar bear population. On trophic and herbivory fronts, invasive species were shown to disrupt size-spectrum relationships in freshwater fish communities, while non-native urban trees in New York City hosted markedly fewer galling specialists than natives despite similar generalist herbivory. Invasion biology highlighted rapid trait evolution in an invasive plant across a latitudinal gradient and the role of reduced litter allelochemicals in facilitating alien-species co-occurrence. Restoration ecology delivered encouraging signals, with drained fen rewetting recovering key species and function, and bee-community recovery in restored agroecosystems assessed through a new recovery-debt framework.
